The early life history of the brown mussel Perna perna begins with a brief embryonic period following gamete fusion. Within approximately 48 hours after fertilisation, at a water temperature of 21 °C [T = 21 °C], the newly hatched D-larvae emerge from the egg capsule, marking the age at birth of 2 days [ab = 2 days]. At this stage of initial shell secretion, the prodissoconch length measures just 0.008822 cm [Lb = 0.008822 cm], representing the shell length at birth. The corresponding wet weight at birth is an exceptionally minute 0.0000000269 grams [Wwb = 0.0000000269 grams], reflecting the lecithotrophic dependence of the early veliger larva on its endogenous yolk reserves. This rapid transition from egg to free-swimming larva is ecologically critical for pelagic dispersal, and the duration of the developmental window is highly sensitive to thermal conditions, with the 2-day interval contingent upon the 21 °C incubation environment.

The planktonic larval phase of Perna perna is characterised by a sequence of well-defined growth milestones before the critical settlement event. After hatching, the trochophore and subsequently the veliger larva undergo substantial size increases as they transition to planktotrophic feeding. Under the same thermal regime of 21 °C [T = 21 °C] that governed embryonic development, the time since birth at metamorphosis is approximately 12 days since birth , at which point the larva attains the pediveliger stage. At this metamorphic climax, the shell length at metamorphosis is recorded as 0.0255 cm , a dimension consistent with the size range reported for primary settlers. During this morphological transformation, the larva loses its velar cilia and develops a functional gill, reorganisation that enables the shift from a pelagic to a benthic existence as a post-metamorphic juvenile.

Growth trajectories of the post-metamorphic spat are significantly influenced by tidal zonation and local hydrodynamic conditions as the juveniles progress toward reproductive competence. In intertidal populations along the South African coast, the shell length at puberty has been determined to be 2.9 cm [Lp = 2.9 cm], a size that generally corresponds to mussels between 25 and 30 mm in shell dimension. Estimates derived from subtidal growth curves suggest that the time since birth at puberty is approximately 100 days since birth [tp = approximately 100 days since birth] when water temperatures average 24 °C [T = 24 °C]. This relatively rapid attainment of sexual maturation allows cohorts settling during optimal thermal windows to contribute to the spawning population within the same season. The onset of gametogenesis at this shell size represents the initiation of reproductive effort, after which individuals enter the sexually mature adult phase and begin allocating resources toward gonad development.

Field measurements from spawning populations indicate a gonadosomatic index (GSI) of 60% [GSI = 60%] when ambient water temperatures reach 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. In terms of shell growth, ultimate shell length in this species has been recorded at 12 cm [Li = 12 cm] in subtidal habitats, though intertidal individuals more typically attain maximum lengths of approximately 9 to 10 cm, with low-intertidal specimens reaching 9.9 cm. This pronounced size disparity likely reflects the greater feeding time available to continuously submerged individuals compared to those subject to aerial exposure during low tide, which constrains both filtration activity and energy acquisition.

Longevity in Perna perna exhibits marked variation depending on the degree of wave exposure. In sheltered South African populations, the maximum recorded lifespan is approximately 9 years [am = approximately 9 years] under a mean annual water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C], whereas individuals on exposed coasts typically survive only 2 to 3 years, likely due to increased physical stress and greater predation pressure. This extended lifespan of nearly a decade in protected embayments permits multiple reproductive seasons, contributing to population resilience. The temperature sensitivity of larval development is further illustrated by the time to puberty, where a duration of 100 days since birth [tp = 100 days since birth] at sustained temperatures around 24 °C [T = 24 °C] is necessary to reach the size threshold for maturation, a timeline that aligns with the subtidal growth curves originally used to derive the Lp threshold of 2.9 cm. Collectively, these life-history parameters position Perna perna as a moderately fast-growing, iteroparous bivalve capable of high reproductive output during favourable thermal windows, with demographic outcomes modulated by local environmental gradients in temperature and exposure.
